newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada crack down on telemarketing scams.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada crack down on telemarketing scams.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission and a group of state and Canadian securities regulators on Wednesday launched a campaign to chip away at some $40 billion in annual investor losses caused by telemarketing scams.

Dubbed "Project Field of Schemes," the plan is aimed at telemarketing ploys used to lure investors into sham investments. The crusade is being undertaken jointly by securities regulators from 21 states, two Canadian provinces and the Federal Trade Commission.

Regulators warned that investment scams have become even more of a concern because many investors are now being enticed by schemes on the Internet, which offers a broader range of potential victims than the typical unsuspecting senior citizens who are often targeted by telephone.

"No one is policing those channels," said Mark Griffin, president of the North American Securities Administrators Association, representing state and Canadian securities regulators. "The Internet in very reduced terms is like a huge classified ad system that goes global."

Teresa Schwartz, deputy director of the FTC's Bureau of Protection, said telemarketing scam artists are becoming more powerful and effective in luring consumers into bogus investments. She said that in nine cases alone consumers may have paid more than $150 million into these schemes.
"They tout high profits and make it believable," she said. "They package their claims in glossy publications and use high-pressure sales pitches that emphasise the need to act quickly."
The regulators began their latest crackdown, six months in the making, with a series of enforcement actions slapped on a broad range of investment scams.
The regulators said the 61 cases include Ostrich ranching in Idaho, retirement investments for the clergy in Maryland and snail farming in Nebraska.

"These schemes run the gamut from worthless oil and gas programmes in Kentucky, and digital fingerprint identification technology in Indiana, to nonexistent Internet sites in California," Griffin said.
In some cases, investors were promised returns as high as 600 percent on their investments.
Some promoters were charged with using money from new investors to pay high returns to earlier investors in what are known as "ponzi," or pyramid, schemes.

For instance, consumers who visited the Web site of a Tucson, Ariz., company read that they could earn up to $2,250 a week in a jewelry marketing programme, when in fact, the FTC said, the operation was really a pyramid scheme.
Griffin warned that recent market conditions have made investors more gullible.
"With the rising bull market in legitimate stocks providing historic returns, too many people are willing to believe the unbelievable," Griffin warned.
He added that consumers are losing more from investment scheme pitches than from any other telemarketing scams.
In one case, promoters for two operations in Sherman Oaks, Calif., lured consumers into buying $15,000 investment units in companies that were purportedly raising cash to reopen a Colorado gold mine.
The FTC said the marketers projected as much as a 1,000 percent return on investment and attracted investors with misrepresentations about the federal government's review of the mining project.
The regulators said that, in addition to pursuing the perpetrators of scams, they also wanted to educate consumers and offered a package of common-sense tips.
The group told consumers especially to be on guard against unsolicited phone calls regarding investments.
As part of the crackdown, regulators called on consumers to alert the FTC's Consumer Response Centre of any questionable offerings by calling 202 326-3128.
